newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Union at Russia's Norilsk nickel adopts strike plan.
newsitem.headline: Union at Russia's Norilsk nickel adopts strike plan.

text.p: Workers at the flagship plant of Russia's giant Norilsk Nickel group approved a strike plan over wage arrears, a union official said on Monday, but the company said it could not meet their payment demands.
A spokesman for Norilsk Nickel, which is called RAO Norilsky Nickel in Russian, said he did not think any strike would result in total production stoppages at the firm's mining and processing plant.
Boris Degtyaryov, deputy head of the plant's main union, the United Trade Union committee, said earlier that a strike would be called if the company failed to meet workers' demands within 10 days.
The timing of any strike and the number of workers involved still had to be decided by a committee coordinating talks with management, he said.

But at least 50,000 workers involved in production and processing of non-ferrous and precious metals could lay down their tools. The maximum number of workers involved would be 120,000 -- the plant's entire workforce, he said.

Norilsk group spokesman Anatoly Komrakov played down the possibility of widescale action, adding: "We have good workers at the plant who know it is not in their interests to undertake such an action."

Another company spokesman, Sergei Vetchinin, said earlier that management at Norilsk, one of the world's most important producers of nickel, cobalt and platinum group metals, could pay off the arrears over this year.
But union officials said the time for paying salary and holiday arrears was too long."The period which the trade union is demanding for repayment is objectively impossible," Vetchinin said.
Norilsk Nickel accounts for nearly 20 percent of annual world nickel supply and 60 percent of palladium supplies.
Prices of nickel, platinum and palladium have risen in recent weeks on concerns over Norilsk supplies.
The comments by Vetchinin and by the union followed a March 1 meeting of labour and management representatives in the inhospitable town of Norilsk, 320 km (200 miles) north of the Arctic Circle.
Vetchinin said the only way payments to workers could be accelerated was by shifting some of the enormous social costs shouldered by the company to the regional Krasnoyarsk budget.
Norilsk says it spent 42 percent of its 1996 revenue on supporting social infrastructure at its company towns.
Vetchinin said company officials were meeting local authorities to ask them to pay for things such as roads and telecommunications in the production towns.

Norilsk's main shareholder, commercial bank Uneximbank, is struggling to implement a rescue package for the metals monolith, which was a showpiece of the Communist planned economy and Moscow's drive to tap metal reserves at any cost.

Degtyaryov said it was not too late to resolve the dispute, adding that the committee should do everything to continue a dialogue with management. "A perfect outcome would be that if all our legitimate demands were met -- there would be no strike," he said.
Russia feeds 25 to 30 percent of western European nickel demand. Stainless steel is the main end-use for nickel, and accounts for around two thirds of nickel consumption.
The Norilsk group owes workers 900 billion roubles ($160 million) in salary and holiday arrears and 1.2 trillion roubles to various budgets.
Workers at the plant have also demanded wages be increased by what RAO Norilsky Nickel has said would cost the company 70 billion roubles a month.
The main metals plant last year produced 100,000 tonnes of nickel from the group's total output of 177,185 tonnes. Total world production is around one million tonnes a year.
